title: Physics of the Eye
lead: The cornea and lens of the eye act together as a single thin lens that forms a real image on the retina. The eye changes its power to keep that image on the retina as an object comes nearer, and the thin lens equations describe that power and the size of the image.
objectives: Explain the image formation by the eye.
Explain why peripheral images lack detail and color.
Analyze the accommodation of the eye for distant and near vision.
summary_html:
• Image formation by the eye is adequately described by the thin lens equations: $P = \frac{1}{\kdobj} + \frac{1}{\kdimg}$ and $\frac{\khimg}{\khobj} = -\frac{\kdimg}{\kdobj} = m$.
  • The eye produces a real image on the retina by adjusting its focal length and power in a process called accommodation.
  • For close vision, the eye is fully accommodated and has its greatest power, whereas for distant vision, it is totally relaxed and has its smallest power.
  • The loss of the ability to accommodate with age is called presbyopia, which is corrected by the use of a converging lens to add power for close vision.
notes: Two of the module’s five problems have no keyed answer and are left out: the power of the eye viewing an object 3.00 m away, and the greatest distance at which a person whose acuity reaches a 4.00 μm image can read 75.0 cm letters on an airplane. The reference to Geometric Optics is plain text, and the book’s “$p=1/f$” keeps its lower-case p as printed.

figures.original_caption: The cornea and lens of an eye act together to form a real image on the light-sensing retina, which has its densest concentration of receptors in the fovea and a blind spot over the optic nerve. The power of the lens of an eye is adjustable to provide an image on the retina for varying object distances. Layers of tissues with varying indices of refraction in the lens are shown here. However, they have been omitted from other pictures for clarity.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 26.3) An image is formed on the retina with light rays converging most at the cornea and upon entering and exiting the lens. Rays from the top and bottom of the object are traced and produce an inverted real image on the retina. The distance to the object is drawn smaller than scale. (Figure 26.4) Relaxed and accommodated vision for distant and close objects. (a) Light rays from the same point on a distant object must be nearly parallel while entering the eye and more easily converge to produce an image on the retina. (b) Light rays from a nearby object can diverge more and still enter the eye. A more powerful lens is needed to converge them on the retina than if they were parallel.

exercises.prompt: A tree that is 3 m tall is viewed from a distance of 25 m. If the cornea-to-retina distance of an ideal eye is 2 cm, how tall is the image of the tree on the observer’s retina?

answer.hint: The image distance is the cornea-to-retina distance, so $\khimg = -\khobj\kdimg/\kdobj$; keep every length in the same unit.

exercises.prompt: Often people with lens-to-retina distances smaller than 2 cm purchase glasses to place in front of their eyes. (a) Explain why people with lens-to-retina distances smaller than 2 cm need glasses. (b) Explain whether the glasses should be composed of converging or diverging lenses. (c) Draw a ray diagram demonstrating the ability to see with and without the glasses.

answer.solution: (a) The cornea and lens of such an eye bring light to a focus about 2 cm behind the lens, but the retina is closer than that, so the rays reach the retina before they meet and the image there is blurred. (b) The eye needs more converging power to bring the rays together sooner, so the glasses should be converging lenses, which add positive power to that of the cornea and lens. (c) Without glasses, draw rays from a point on the object that pass through the eye and cross behind the retina, spreading into a patch where they reach it. With glasses, draw the same rays bent inward by the converging lens first, so that after the cornea and lens they cross exactly on the retina.

exercises.prompt: If the lens of a person’s eye is removed because of cataracts (as has been done since ancient times), why would you expect a spectacle lens of about 16 D to be prescribed?

answer.solution: The cornea supplies about two-thirds of the power of the eye and the lens the remaining third. For an eye of about 50 D, the lens supplies roughly one-third of that, about 16 D. With the lens removed, the eye lacks that power, so a converging spectacle lens of about 16 D is needed to bring the image back onto the retina.

exercises.prompt: A cataract is cloudiness in the lens of the eye. Is light dispersed or diffused by it?

answer.solution: Light is diffused. The cloudiness scatters light in many directions, so rays from one point on an object no longer meet at one point on the retina and the image is hazy. Dispersion is the spreading of light into its colors because the index of refraction depends on wavelength, and that is not what a cataract does.

exercises.prompt: When laser light is shone into a relaxed normal-vision eye to repair a tear by spot-welding the retina to the back of the eye, the rays entering the eye must be parallel. Why?

answer.solution: A relaxed normal eye is focused on very distant objects, whose rays arrive parallel, so it brings parallel rays to a point on the retina. Parallel laser light therefore converges to a small, intense spot exactly on the retina, where the weld is needed. Rays that were not parallel would meet in front of or behind the retina and spread their energy over a larger patch of it.

exercises.prompt: How does the power of a dry contact lens compare with its power when resting on the tear layer of the eye? Explain.

answer.solution: A dry contact lens has air on both sides, and the large difference between the index of the lens and that of air makes rays bend strongly at its surfaces. On the eye, its back surface rests on the tear layer, whose index is close to that of water and of the cornea, so rays bend very little at that surface. The contact lens therefore has a different, smaller effective power on the eye than it has dry in air, and its prescription accounts for this.

exercises.prompt: Why is your vision so blurry when you open your eyes while swimming under water? How does a face mask enable clear vision?

answer.solution: The cornea supplies most of the power of the eye because light slows considerably going from air, $n = 1.0$, into the cornea, $n = 1.38$. Water has $n = 1.33$, nearly the same as the cornea, so under water light hardly bends at the cornea, the eye loses most of its power, and the image forms far behind the retina. A face mask keeps a layer of air in front of the eyes, so light again enters the cornea from air and the cornea regains its power.

exercises.prompt: What is the power of the eye when viewing an object 50.0 cm away?

answer.hint: Use $P = 1/\kdobj + 1/\kdimg$ with both distances in meters and $\kdimg = 0.0200$ m.

exercises.prompt: (a) The print in many books averages 3.50 mm in height. How high is the image of the print on the retina when the book is held 30.0 cm from the eye? (b) Compare the size of the print to the sizes of rods and cones in the fovea and discuss the possible details observable in the letters. (The eye-brain system can perform better because of interconnections and higher order image processing.)

parts.part: (a) the height of the image on the retina
parts.hint: Use $\khimg = -\khobj\kdimg/\kdobj$ with the lens-to-retina distance of 2.00 cm.

answer.solution: (a) $-0.233\ \text{mm}$ (b) The size of the rods and the cones is smaller than the image height, so we can distinguish letters on a page.

exercises.prompt: People who do very detailed work close up, such as jewellers, often can see objects clearly at much closer distance than the normal 25 cm. (a) What is the power of the eyes of a woman who can see an object clearly at a distance of only 8.00 cm? (b) What is the size of an image of a 1.00 mm object, such as lettering inside a ring, held at this distance? (c) What would the size of the image be if the object were held at the normal 25.0 cm distance?
